DOC.EP: EC.01.01.01 The hospital plans activities to minimize risks in the environment of care. Note: One or more persons can be assigned to manage risks associated with the management plans described in this standard. EP 1. Leaders identify an individual(s) to manage risk, coordinate risk reduction activities in the physical environment, collect deficiency in- formation, and disseminate summaries of actions and results. Note: Deficiencies include injuries, problems, or use errors.
DOC.FINDING: The Data Management Program is basically the collection of raw data with limited aggregration and analysis is difficult and at some times impossible. The format for data display is not stand- ardized either by function or department. The horizontal coordination, collaboration, communi- cation and coorperation between Safety, Facilities and Infection Control is limited. Negative interpersonal relationships as identified in February, by the previous consultant, are still in place.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is recommended that Senior Management develop specific measurable goals/objectives and a specific timeline of completion, for each of the leaders of the functions mentioned above and each leader held speciically accountible for the success of the on-time completion of each goal/objective, particularly Joint Commission compliance in their applicable area of responsibilities. A Standard by Standard and Element of Performance Element by Element of Performance review of the Environment of Care function is recommended. This report can be used to prioritize identified areas of limited or partial compliance. This should be completed withing the next thirty (30) days as the hospital is within the window of survey. EP 2. Leaders identify an individual(s) to intervene whenever environ- mental conditions immediately threaten life or health or threaten to dam- age equipment or buildings.
DOC.FINDING: It could not be determined if a currrent letter was on file identifying this individual by title.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Assure that this letter is current and available for Surveyor review, when requested. The hospital has a written plan for managing the following (EPs 3-8): EP 5. Hazardous materials and waste. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 15)
DOC.FINDING: During the Building Tour, there were numerous instances where flamible spray cans were found stored in non approved areas, including construction areas where inspections were supposed to be occuring, but documentation was limited. There is still comparmentalization relating to these inspections and rounds and there is limited effective documentation related to correction of iden- tified deficiencies.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Not only for Hazardous Materials and Waste, but both the consturction inspections and the Weekly Rounds and other rounds procedures should be revised to assure a wider area of coverage of what is reviewed/inspected. A sample Surveillance Rounds form has been sent to the hospital. Those who conduct the rounds should be formally trained on how to conduct the rounds. Additionally, deficiencies should be aggregated by department and include those deficiencies that are reoccuring. This should be reported to the Environment of Care Com- mittee quarterly. Environmental Rounds for the first part of 2010 do not appear to be conducted on a con- sistant basis. Most of the deficiencies identified were minor repair and cleanliness issues and documentation of correction was missing. EP 6. Fire safety. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 15)
DOC.FINDING: See EP 5 above. Penetration repair is an issue in the hospital. During the Building Tour, there were numerous instances where flamible spray cans were found stored in non approved areas, including construction areas where inspections were supposed to be occuring, but documentation was limited. There is still comparmentalization relating to these inspections and rounds and there is limited effective documentation related to correction of iden- tified deficiencies.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: See EP 5 above. Consider the immediate implementation of a Ceiling Permit Program. A copy was sent to the hospital. EP 7. Medical equipment. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 15)
DOC.FINDING: The Department Head for this area is new and is in the process of reviewing all policies and pro- cedures and other aspects of the Biomedical Equipment Program. It could not be determined if the Biomedical Inventory was complete and ratings used to risk assess equipment into the inven- tory are not available as the software program appears to be outdated and has limited flexibility. On various occassions biomedical equipment has been ordered and directly received by the or- dering department, without notifying the Biomedical Department. Several efforts were made to visit with selected individuals in the Purchasing Department relating to this difficulty, but this was unsuccessful. It was explained to the consultant that Service Chiefs and the Research areas were the primary areas where this situation occurred. The practice of biomedical equipment be- ing place in service without an initial inspection by the Biomedical Engineering Department must be stopped. There is basically no surpervision of rental, loaned and borrowed equipment that comes to the hospital, particularly medical equipment supplied by vendors. A policy covering this situation could not be located. The is a serious deficiency.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The new Department Head should continue with his audit of the Biomedical Function and the specific compliance with the applicable Joint Commission Standards. A Rental, Loaned, Borrowed and Patient Owned Equipment Policy and Procedure should be developed and im- plemented. Because of the size of the Biomedical Program and the many gaps in compli- ance and documentation, it is recommed that this area, along with several other areas men- tioned in this report, be resurveyed. The completed evaluation should be completed within the next thirty (30) days. EP 8. Utility systems. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 15)
DOC.FINDING: This Utility Management Progam is a functional program that appears to be working well, but time did not premit an in depth review, including a review of drawings and utility emergency operation plans.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: A complete review should be completed.

DOC.EP: EC.02.01.01 The hospital manages safety and security risks. EP 1. The hospital identifies safety and security risks associated with the environment of care. Note: Risks are identified from internal sources such as ongoing moni- toring of the environment, results of root cause analyses, results of an- nual proactive risk assessments of high-risk processes, and from credible external sources such as Sentinel Event Alerts. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 14)
DOC.FINDING: There has not been a formal Security Risk Assessment completed for either of these areas.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is recommended that a Security Risk Assessment, including grounds, be completed as soon as possible. One this assessessment is completed, identified risks must have a wirtten Action Plan and plan for monitoring once the plan(s) are implemented. Documentation of corrective actions and dated of completion must be included. Though not required, it is rec- ommended that these Risk Assessments and Action Plans be sent to the Environment of Care Committee for review and monitoring, on a monthly basis, as necessary. EP 3. The hospital takes action to minimize or eliminate identified safe- ty and security risks in the physical environment.
DOC.FINDING: Safety risks are partially identified through Environmental Tours/Safety Surveillance Rounds, but the raw data is not aggregated and reoccuring deficiencies and correction of identified defi- ciencies is not consistently monitored. Data requested for Security was not available for review. Rounds for the first part of 2010 appear to be conducted inconsistently.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Both the Safety and Security Risk Assessments are formal processes and should be complet- ed as soon as possible. It is recommended that these assessments have Corrective Action Plans be completed and recommendations from the action plans implement as soon as possi- ble. This should be reported and reviewed monthly by the Environment of Care Committee. EP 5. The hospital maintains all grounds and equipment.
DOC.FINDING: All grounds appear to be well maintained, but requested documentation of grounds rounds was not available.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is recommended that a formal Grounds Risk Assessment be conducted, at least on a monthly basis. This may be currently accomplished by the Police Department, but the in- formation was not available for review. It is important that identified deficiencies be cor- rected and there must be clear documentation of when the deficiency was corrected. EP 7. The hospital identifies individuals entering its facilities. Note: The hospital determines which of those individuals require identi- fication and how to do so.
DOC.FINDING: Though the hosptial has strict security at the front door reqiring the review of identification of all visitors, several vendors and one individual that appeared to be a contractor, did not have a name tag. There is limited horizontal communication between the Campus Police Department and the compliance of the Security and Emergency Mangement sections of the Joint Commission re- quirements. Though compliance may fall to someone else outside of the Police Department, in two visits with the Police Department there was limited understanding of the correlation of Lock Down Procedures and Emergency Management.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is recommended that the Vendor and Contractor badge program be reviewed to assure that the policies and procedures are correct and are being strickly followed. The Emergency Management Program is being rebuilt and a new coordinator has been recently employed. Attention should be focused on assuring a clear and seamless coordination, communication, calaboration and cooperation between the Police Department and the Emergency Manage- ment Program. Being a member of the Emergency Management Committee does not assure that this will occur EP 8. The hospital controls access to and from areas it identifies as secu- rity sensitive.
DOC.FINDING: Checks of all magnetic doors are currently underway.
DOC.RECOMMENDED:
This should include all satellite facilities, including the Research building ant the inspection completed within the next thirty (30) days. EP 9. The hospital has written procedures to follow in the event of a se- curity incident, including an infant or pediatric abduction.
Though there is limited children in the facility it is recommended that a Lost/Missing Child policy and procedure be incorpored in the the Facility Lockdown Procedure. This should be drilled with in the 3rd Quarter and fully critiqued. The Facility Lockdown Policy and Procedure was discussed with a representative of the Campus Police Department and the policy does not appear to include an event of a lost or possible abducted child. EP 10. When a security incident occurs, the hospital follows its identi- fied procedures.
DOC.FINDING: The security incidents reviewed were not in a aggregated format. It is recommed that an Aggregated Security Incident Report be sent to the Enviroment of Care Committee on a regulary basis. The Police Department should make recommendations of what will be sub- mitted, but the Committed should have final approval. EP 11. The hospital responds to product notices and recalls. (See also MM.05.01.17, EPs 1-4) Several recall notices were traced and there are gaps in receiving verification back from the de- partments that received the recall notice from the hospital.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is important that for every notice sent out to departments, by the hospital, that specific in- formation is received back verifying that they do or do not have the product related to the particular recall. Serious consideration should be given to having one place for all Recall Notices to be coordinated. This would allow for a central file of all recall notices; equip- ment, medication, food, etc. Aggregated information should be compiled and submitted to the Environment of Care Committee, Quality Management Committee or other appropriate committee.

DOC.EP: EC.02.01.03 The hospital prohibits smoking except in specific circumstances. EP 1. The hospital develops a written policy prohibiting smoking in all buildings. Exceptions for patients in specific circumstances are defined.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The hospital should be commended for their smoking enforcement program as the consultant did not find a single violation of this policy. EP 4. If the hospital decides that patients may smoke in specific circum- stances, it designates smoking areas that are physically separate from care, treatment, and service areas. (See also EC.02.03.01, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: A medical record was not reviewed of a patient that was approved to smoke inside the hospital. A roof top designated smoking was visited and was found to be clean and no violations were identified.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: EP 6. The hospital takes action to maintain compliance with its smoking policy.

DOC.EP: EC.02.02.01 The hospital manages risks related to hazardous materials and waste. EP 1. The hospital maintains a written, current inventory of hazardous materials and waste that it uses, stores, or generates. The only materials that need to be included on the inventory are those whose handling, use, and storage are addressed by law and regulation. (See also IC.02.01.01, EP 6; MM.01.01.03, EP 3)
DOC.FINDING: MSDS Sheets in some departments are not updated on a regular basis.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The hospital should explore purchasing an on-line MSDS sheet on demand service. This will enable the MSDS sheets to be continually updated and staff could access by the internet and/or 800 number. MSDS sheets would not have to be maintained at the department level unless there is a VISN or Central Office directive requiring the sheets be available at the de- partmemental level. Hospitals that have implemented this programs have found it to be ef- fective and has reduced staff time considerbly in maintaining the program.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.01 The hospital manages fire risks. EP 1. The hospital minimizes the potential for harm from fire, smoke, and other products of combustion.
DOC.FINDING: Flammable spray cans were found in five separate areas, including one construction site.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is recommended that the Environmental Tour/Surveillance Rounds report be expanded to include more items to review and include looking for flammable spray cans and other flam- mable and explosive products, EP 2. If patients are permitted to smoke, the hospital takes measures to minimize fire risk. (See also EC.02.01.03, EP 4)
DOC.FINDING: Smoking is allowed only in designated smoking areas, located outside the hospital, unless ap- proved in selected circumstances as outlined in a policy. The consultant did not find a patient that had this approval.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: During the actual Survey, all patients that have approval to smoke inside the hospital should have their medical record review to assure that it meet all aspects of this policy. EP 4. The hospital maintains free and unobstructed access to all exits. Note: This requirement applies to all buildings classified as business oc- cupancy. The "Life Safety" (LS) chapter addresses the requirements for all other occupancy types.
DOC.FINDING: Numerous halls, throughout the hospital and Research building, that are used for primary egress, were found blocked by equipment, storage and clutter. This has been identified as an issue in various reports reviewed. The hospital certainly has a space problem, but this is a good example of items being identified as not in compliance, month after month, and the issue has not been resolved.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The hospitall has a seirous space problem and there does not appear to be a Senior Leader- ship directed approach to space management, though it was mentioned to the consultant that there were plans in current construction to afford some relief for this issue. Just asking de- partments to move the equipment has not proven to be effective. The space problem should be reviewed in detail and a written master plan for: disposal of old and/or unused equipment and storage of equipment used intermittently. Assuring that all primary means of egress halls are clear and unobstructed, should be a top priority as this will result in multiple RFI's if not corrected. EP 10. The written fire response plan describes the specific roles of staff and licensed independent practitioners at and away from a fire's point of origin, including when and how to sound fire alarms, how to contain smoke and fire, how to use a fire extinguisher, and how to evacuate to areas of refuge. (See also EC.02.03.03, EP 5)
DOC.FINDING: It was not clear in the plans reviewed that the specific roles of Licensed Independent Practition- ers, students and volunteers at or away from the fire's point of orgin is fully covered. Testing of this with the LIP's, students and volunteers is either not done or is not well documented.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is recommended that the Fire Response Plan and particularly all Departmental Plans be reviewed to assure that this requirment related to specific roles is clearly covered. The accu- racy of the Department Fire Plans should also be verified.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.03 The hospital conducts fire drills. EP 1. The hospital conducts fire drills once per shift per quarter in each building defined as a health care occupancy by the Life Safety Code. The hospital conducts quarterly fire drills in each building defined as an am- bulatory health care occupancy by the Life Safety Code. (See also LS.01.02.01, EP 11; LS.02.01.70, EP 4; LS.03.01.70, EP 6) Note 1: Evacuation of patients during drills is not required. Note 2: In leased or rented facilities, drills need be conducted only in areas of the building that the hospital occupies.
DOC.FINDING: Fire drills in fall of 2009 were inconsistently conducted. Drill critiques in the clinics were also inconsistent and not completed on a timely basis. Fire Drill critiques reviewed, particularly in the Clinics, were very basic. One critique was returned three months after the drill was conduct- ed. Other Fire Drill critiques were incomplete and/or had deficiencies listed without documenta- tion of correction or other remedial action such as staff eduction.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Fire drill critiques should be completed within 2-3 working days and this should be outlined in a specific policy. The critique form should be reviewed for completeness and efficacy and evaluate all aspects of the drill. Identified deficiencies should be aggregated and used as a teaching tool to permanently correct these deficiencies. This should be regularly reported, in an aggregated format to the Environment of Care Committee. EP 2. The hospital conducts fire drills every 12 months from the date of the last drill in all freestanding buildings classified as business occupan- cies and in which patients are seen or treated. Note: In leased or rented facilities, drills need be conducted only in are- as of the building that the hospital occupies.
DOC.FINDING: The information furnished related to fire drills in areas classified as Business Occupancy indi- cated that drills were not conducted nor critiqued on a timely basis, in some clinic areas.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Fire drills should be conducted and coordinated by one individual and critiques returned to them within 2-3 working days. Aggregated results, including deficiencies should be includ- ed. EP 4. Staff who work in buildings where patients are housed or treated participate in drills according to the hospital’s fire response plan. Note: When drills are conducted between 9:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m., the hospital may use alternative methods to notify staff instead of activating the building's fire alarm system.
DOC.FINDING: As mentioned earlier, some fire drills were not conducted or evaluated on a timely basis.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Fire drills should be conducted and coordinated by one individual and critiques returned to them within 2-3 working days. Aggregated results, including deficiencies should be includ- ed. EP 5. The hospital critiques fire drills to evaluate fire safety equipment, fire safety building features, and staff response to fire. The evaluation is documented. (See also EC.02.03.01, EP 10)
DOC.FINDING: Some fire drill critiques were incomplete.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is recommended that a log be developed to assure all areas expected to complete critiques and return them on a timely basis. Results should be reported to and followed by the Envi- ronment of Care Committee.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.05 The hospital maintains fire safety equipment and fire safety building features. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of fire safety equipment and building features described below. However, if these types of equipment or features exist with- in the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 1. At least quarterly, the hospital tests supervisory signal devices (except valve tamper switches). The completion date of the tests is doc- umented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2).
DOC.FINDING: Time constraints did not allow for a full review of compliance with the required Life Safety in- spections. Two documents (one the hospital had, but was not using) that can be used to do a complete Life Safety document evaluation were sent to the hospital.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is recommended that at least two Life Safety Document checks be conducted in the next two months, the first as soon as possible and the second to check that any identified defi- ciencies that were identifed have been corrected. Those that will be with the Life Safety Survey and all back-ups should be involved. Some of the inspections were in process and/or had been scheduled and a completed evalua- tion could not be made. It is important that when a Life Safety deficiency or failure is identified by the company do- ing the inspection is noted and there is written evidence that the deficiency was not only cor- rected, but retested and the date. It is important that only the information requested by the Surveyor is submitted. Some of the books contained inspections and information as far back as 2006. It appears that this li- brary of Life Safety Documentation has recently been completed and those involved in this laborious task should be commended.

DOC.EP: EC.02.04.01 The hospital manages medical equipment risks. EP 1. The hospital solicits input from individuals who operate and ser- vice equipment when it selects and acquires medical equipment. EP 2. The hospital maintains either a written inventory of all medical equipment or a written inventory of selected equipment categorized by physical risk associated with use (including all life-support equipment) and equipment incident history. The hospital evaluates new types of equipment before initial use to determine whether they should be includ- ed in the inventory. (See also EC.02.04.03, EPs 1 and 3)
DOC.FINDING: There is an new Department Head who is in the process of conducting a top to bottom audit of the Department. The Biomedical Inventory is maintained by an outdated software program and it could not be determined the point value of what determined the equipment to be included or excluded in the Medical Equipment Inventory. The Loaned, Borrowed, Rental, Physicial, Patient and Vendor furnished medical equipment Pol- icy and Procedure was not available for review and may not be an approved policy. The hospital does have a Risk Assessment procedure for evaluating equipment to determine if it is to be included in the Biomedical Equipment Inventory. This should include a point value for equipment evaluated to assist in determing the frequency of preventative maintenance inspec- tions.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Continue the Policy and Procedure review and revision currently being conducted. A Loaned, Borrowed, Rental, Physicial, Patient and Vendor furnished medical equipment Policy and Procedure should be developed and implemented as soon as possible. All medical equipment purchases should be coordinated with the Biomedical Department so they will be able to negotiate schematics and training program for staff, before the contract is signed and to assure the equipment is inspected before conducting patient care. Vendors bringing medical equipment into the hospital should notify the Biomedical Depart- ment before the equipment is demonstrated and/or used in patient care-no exceptions. The Biomedical Section should be resurveyed to measure progress and compliance of what has been implemented.. EP 3. The hospital identifies the activities, in writing, for maintaining, inspecting, and testing for all medical equipment on the inventory. (See also EC.02.04.03, EPs 2 and 3) Note: Hospitals may use different strategies for different items as appro- priate. For example, strategies such as predictive maintenance, reliabil- ity-centered maintenance, interval-based inspections, corrective mainte- nance, or metered maintenance may be selected to ensure reliable per- formance.
DOC.FINDING: Medical Equipment preventive maintenance inspections due vs. those completed on time appear to be somewhat low. There is a problem with trying to locate equipment due inspections and this amount is increas- ing. There is not a written policy relating when a piece of equipment that can not be located, is taken out of the Medical Equipment Inventory.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Though there is no specic benchmark related to inspections conducted on time, it is recom- mended that an on time inspection rate of at least 98% be maintained on a regular basis. A week to "sweep the hospital" for missing equiment should be conducted that involves all staff and departments. Rewarding anyone that finds a piece of missing equipment would re- ceive a coupon for a free lunch in the cafeteria or other reward(s). A policy must be developed and implemented on when a piece of medical equipment can be removed from the medical equipment inventory. The consultant recommends consideration of a timeframe of at least ninety (90) days. If the equipment has been lost or stolen, it should not continue to bring down the biomedical preventative maintenance inspection rates. If the equipment is located, it can be inspected and returned to the active inventory. EP 4. The hospital identifies, in writing, frequencies for inspecting, test- ing, and maintaining medical equipment on the inventory based on crite- ria such as manufacturers’ recommendations, risk levels, or current hos- pital experience. (See also EC.02.04.03, EPs 2 and 3)
DOC.FINDING: The hospital has a Risk Assessment evaluation of including a piece of equipment into or exclud- ing from the medical equipment inventory. The point value of the equipment rating cannot be determined. This is a serious deficiency
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The point value should determined so the frequency of inspections can be determined. The Biomedical Department Head is aware of this concern and is reviewing information to see if the current software can be used to determine the point values. EP 5. The hospital monitors and reports all incidents in which medical equipment is suspected in or attributed to the death, serious injury, or serious illness of any individual, as required by the Safe Medical Devices Act of 1990.
DOC.FINDING: Several recall notices were traced and there are gaps in receiving verification back from the de- partments that received the recall notice.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is important that for every notice sent out to departments, that specific information is re- ceived back in a set periond of time verifying that they do or do not have the product(s) re- lated to the recall. Serious consideration should be given to have one place for all Recall Notices to be coordinated. Time frame should be no longer than five (5) days. This would allow for a central file of all recall notices; equipment, medication, food, etc. EP 6. The hospital has written procedures to follow when medical equipment fails, including using emergency clinical interventions and backup equipment.
DOC.FINDING: Staff were inconsistent in their answers of what procedures to follow if a critical piece of medi- cal equipment failed. A policy and procedure covering this situation could not be located.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: It is important that staff, as appropriate, be fully aware of what steps to follow when medical equipment fails. The appropriate procedure should be detailed, implemented and staff edu- cated accordingly. This should be tested during Surveillance Rounds.

DOC.EP: EC.02.04.03 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains medical equipment. EP 1. Before initial use of medical equipment on the medical equipment inventory, the hospital performs safety, operational, and functional checks. (See also EC.02.04.01, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: Equipment is still being ordered, received and placed into service without involving the Biomed- ical Equipment Department. Service Chiefs and the Research Areas appear to be causing part of the difficulty. Materials Management did not appear to be actively involved in assuring that Bi- omedical was involved in this process.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: A Policy and Procudure should be developed and implemented to assure this practice is stopped. Materials Management should be assuring that Biomedical is notified as medical equipment is ordered and received, before delivering to the department. This is a serious de- ficiency and should be corrected as soon as possible. EP 2. The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains all life-support equip- ment. These activities are documented. (See also EC.02.04.01, EPs 3 and 4; PC.02.01.11, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: As noted above, there is a problem with locating all equipment in the inventory to assure that preventative maintenance inspections are conducted on time and ALL biomedical equipment ordered is inspected before deliveirng to the department and is used in patient care.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Specific steps, including developing and implementing a policy and procedure requiring that the Biomedical Department be involved in checking all equipment, before being used on a patient. The "Unable to Locate" equipment is growing and a policy should be developed relating to when a piece of equipment that cannot be located can be removed from the Biomedical In- ventory. EP 3. The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains non–life-support equipment identified on the medical equipment inventory. These activi- ties are documented. (See also EC.02.04.01, EPs 2-4 and PC.02.01.11, EP 2) EP 4. The hospital conducts performance testing of and maintains all sterilizers. These activities are documented. (See also IC.02.02.01, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: Maintenance documentation was not reviewed.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The sterilizer maintenance logs should be reviewed to assure the preventive maintenance inspections are completed on time. EP 5. The hospital performs equipment maintenance and chemical and biological testing of water used in hemodialysis. These activities are documented. EP 14. For hospitals that use Joint Commission accreditation for deemed status purposes: Qualified hospital staff inspect, test, and cali- brate nuclear medicine equipment annually. The dates of these activities are documented.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.01 The hospital manages risks associated with its utility systems. EP 1. The hospital designs and installs utility systems that meet patient care and operational needs. (See also EC.02.06.05, EP 1) EP 2. The hospital maintains a written inventory of all operating com- ponents of utility systems or maintains a written inventory of selected operating components of utility systems based on risks for infection, oc- cupant needs, and systems critical to patient care (including all life- support systems). The hospital evaluates new types of utility components before initial use to determine whether they should be included in the inventory. (See also EC.02.05.05, EPs 1, 3-5)
DOC.FINDING: The department is still in the process of updating the utility inventory. Time constraints did not allow for a complete review of the Utility Management Program.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Continue the update and once completed a test of the on time completion of preventative maintenance should be completed. A level of at least 98% on time completion should be achieved and maintained. EP 3. The hospital identifies, in writing, inspection and maintenance ac- tivities for all operating components of utility systems on the inventory. (See also EC.02.05.05, EPs 3 - 5; EC.02.05.09, EP 1) Note: Hospitals may use different approaches to maintenance. For ex- ample, activities such as predictive maintenance, reliability-centered maintenance, interval-based maintenance, corrective maintenance, or metered maintenance may be selected to ensure dependable perfor- mance.
DOC.FINDING: The department is still in the process of updating the utility inventory.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Continue the update and once completed a test of the on time completion of preventative maintenance should be completed. A level of at least 98% on time completion should be achieved and maintained. EP 4. The hospital identifies, in writing, the intervals for inspecting, testing, and maintaining all operating components of the utility systems on the inventory, based on criteria such as manufacturers' recommenda- tions, risk levels, or hospital experience. (See also EC.02.05.05, EPs 3-5) EP 5. The hospital minimizes pathogenic biological agents in cooling towers, domestic hot-and cold-water systems, and other aerosolizing wa- ter systems. Maintenance of the cooling towers should be reviewed to assure that it is completed on time and deficiencies are document as corrected and retested. The primary concern is Legionella and Infection Control should be aware of the tower maintenance. EP 6. In areas designed to control airborne contaminants (such as bio- logical agents, gases, fumes, dust), the ventilation system provides ap- propriate pressure relationships, air-exchange rates, and filtration effi- ciencies. Note: Areas designed for control of airborne contaminants include spac- es such as operating rooms, special procedure rooms, delivery rooms for patients diagnosed with or suspected of having airborne communicable diseases (for example, pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis), patients in "protective environment" rooms (for example, those receiving bone mar- row transplants), laboratories, pharmacies, and sterile supply rooms. For further information, see Guidelines for Design and Construction of Hospitals and Health Care Facilities, 2001 edition, published by the American Institute of Architects.
DOC.FINDING:
Several tests were noted where a room had failed and there was not documentation what had been corrected and very impotantly that the new repair/part was retested and that this is fully documented. EP 10. The hospital's procedures address shutting off the malfunctioning system and notifying staff in affected areas.
Some staff were not sure whose responsibility it was to turn off medical gasses during a fire emergency.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: This should be covered in New Employee and Departmental Orientation and tested during Surveillance Rounds. EP 11. The hospital's procedures address performing emergency clinical interventions during utility system disruptions.
DOC.FINDING: The policies and procedures, including departmental policies and procedures, are currently un- der review and being updated as appropriate.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Continue the review and once completed, staff should be tested to assure their responsibilites are fully understood.

DOC.EP: EC.02.06.01 The hospital establishes and maintains a safe, functional environment. Note: The environment is constructed, arranged, and maintained to foster patient safety, pro- vide facilities for diagnosis and treatment, and provide for special services appropriate to the needs of the community. EP 20. Areas used by patients are clean and free of offensive odors.
DOC.FINDING: The consultants noted numerous areas in the hospital that had horizontal dust. Examples include many drip trays under foam hand gel containers, vending machines, offices and furniture and patient rooms. Corners in rest rooms were unclean, toilet seat wipe containers were empty in three rest rooms (one for four days), paper towel dispensers were packed so tightly towels could be removed only in pieces which was thrown on the floor. Base boards and bumper guards, par- ticularly on the ground floor were dirty. Elevator tracks had heavy accumulation of dirt and de- bris in the tracks and on the sevice elevator was very, very dirty. (Tracks and cab of this elevator was cleaned the day after the Building Tour. DOC.EP: EC.02.06.05 The hospital manages its environment during demolition, renovation, or new construction to reduce risk to those in the organization. EP 2. When planning for demolition, construction, or renovation, the hospital conducts a preconstruction risk assessment for air quality re- quirements, infection control, utility requirements, noise, vibration, and other hazards that affect care, treatment, and services. Note: See LS.01.02.01 for information on fire safety procedures to im- plement during construction or renovation.
DOC.FINDING: The Infection Control Risk Assessment (ICRA) is completed, but there is no identification of who will conduct inspections, the frequency or who will maintain the data from the inspections. Inspections when Interim Life Safety Management (ILSM) is implemented are not consistently completed nor documented. Coordination, communication, cooperation and collaboration be- tween Facility Management, Safety and Infection must be improved immediately.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: There are multiple construction and remodeling projects underway and in the planning phase. Surveyors will look at the Infection Control Risk Assessment (ICRA), Interim Life Safety Management (ILSM), documentation of inspections and fire safety compliance will be a central focus of the Life Safety Surveyor. Documentation and coordination between departments must be outstanding to avoid various RFI's, some that will also be assigned un- der the Leadership Chapter which equals 2+ RFI's per deficiency. Documentation of all construction and remodeling projects, including inspections, should be reviewed at least twice in the next 60 days. The ICRA and ILSM forms should include a space for who, by title, should conduct inspec- tions and the frequency of the inspections. Aggregation of the inspection results should be completed and regularly reported to the Environment of Care Committee. This is a serious deficiency and should be corrected immediately. EP 3. The hospital takes action based on its assessment to minimize risks during demolition, construction, or renovation.
DOC.FINDING: This will remain in non compliance until the consistency and quality of the inspections men- tioned above is improved.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: Continue to refine and improve the process related to the ICRA and ILSM inspections until it is a seamless and effective process. Departmental silos, particularly between Facility Management and Safety are preventing the program from being effective. Infection Contorl should be more actively involved and focus should be more than just the ICRA.

DOC.EP: EC.04.01.01 The hospital collects information to monitor conditions in the environment. EP 1. The hospital establishes a process(es) for continually monitoring, internally reporting, and investigating the following: Injuries to patients or others within the hospital’s facilities Occupational illnesses and staff injuries Incidents of damage to its property or the property of others Security incidents involving patients, staff, or others within its facili- ties Hazardous materials and waste spills and exposures Fire safety management problems, deficiencies, and failures Medical or laboratory equipment management problems, failures, and use errors Utility systems management problems, failures, or use errors Note 1: All the incidents and issues listed above may be reported to staff in quality assessment, improvement, or other functions. A summary of such incidents may also be shared with the person designated to coordi- nate safety management activities. Note 2: Review of incident reports often requires that legal processes be followed to preserve confidentiality. Opportunities to improve care, treatment, or services, or to prevent similar incidents, are not lost as a result of following the legal process.
DOC.FINDING: Large amounts of raw data is being collected not only in the Environment of Care, but all over the hospital and in most cases, particularly in the Environment of Care, nothing is being done with the data; limited aggregation, making analysis and monitoring of Corrective Action Plans difficult. Rounds are being conducted weekly, deficiencies noted and this information is sent to the ap- propriate Department Heads, but there is limited follow-up and no tracking of reoccuring defi- ciencies. The overall Environment of Care, including Safety, is not being consistenly nor completely evaluated. Most information that is being sent to the Enviorment of Care Committee is not aggregated and results in pages and pages of raw date. It is difficult to track and trend this data which makes the Committee less effective. Additionally, minutes are not consistant in tracking closed and open items or follow-up on action items.
